items.body: I am silver and exact I am not cruel, only truthful I have looked at it so long I think it is a part of my heart Now I am a lake Ora Sono Un Lago is an album that unfolds through reflection, in every sense of the word. Borrowing its title from Sylvia Plath’s Mirror, where the mirror transforms into a lake, Bono / Burattini construct a record concerned with self-examination, memory and transformation, balancing stillness and movement with poise. The title track immediately makes a bold statement. Rather than functioning as a mere introduction, it plunges the listener straight into a cinematic burst of synthesizers, drawing on the tradition of kosmische music. It is a sink-or-swim opening that establishes the album’s broad horizon from the outset. What follows is a gradual process of discovery. “Prove d’esistenza / Il gesto” finds the duo feeling their way forward through the interaction between Francesca Bono’s Moog Mother-32 and Vittoria Burattini’s highly physical drumming. The piece embraces experimentation and gesture, allowing patterns and textures to emerge organically rather than forcing them into fixed forms. Elsewhere, “Acrobata” introduces a subtle sense of unease, its eerie breaths and spectral vocalisations unsettling the album’s otherwise luminous surface. Throughout the record, Bono and Burattini move effortlessly between progressive electronics, minimalist repetition, soundtrack sensibilities and acoustic intimacy. Tracks such as “Come un riflesso” embody the album’s fascination with dialogue: between machine and performer, acoustic and electronic sound, spontaneity and manipulation. The result often recalls Italian genre cinema, library music and electronic experimentation without ever becoming nostalgic. The closing sequence brings a shift in emotional perspective. If the album begins submerged within the lake, “Oltre le Palpebre” and the beautiful “Lonely Blue Star” gradually look upward. The latter, inspired by the rare astronomical phenomenon of a star surviving beyond its expected lifespan, becomes a fitting metaphor for endurance and transcendence. As synths, percussion and guitar drift into open space, “Ora Sono un Lago” arrives at a place of quiet acceptance. It is a record that understands reflection as a form of movement, water that appears still while carrying unseen currents beneath the surface. photo by Antonietta Dicorato We are grateful that Francesca Bono and Vittoria Burattini were at hand to helps us see beyond the reflection. The title Ora Sono Un Lago comes from Sylvia Plath’s poem “Mirror”, where the mirror transforms into a lake, becoming a space of reflection, truth, and self-confrontation. What drew you to that particular image, and how does it resonate with the emotional and musical landscape of the album? Francesca: The long process that usually leads to the creation of an album is influenced by external stimuli, which can stem from one’s private and social life, from political events around the world, from reading, experiences, and much more. From this melting pot, certain things sometimes break away, drifting ever closer to your orbit until they stick to you—and that’s exactly what happened with certain words written by Sylvia Plath and Patrizia Cavalli, two literary figures who kept us company during the making of the record. Certain lines kept echoing and reverberating as we were composing, and it seemed to me that they said a lot about what we were writing, musically. So, we happened to bring them up again while we were putting together the demos for the various tracks, and I felt a strong pull toward them. Of course, the title we chose is also a meditation on the passing of time, and the role it plays in the life and output of musicians, especially female musicians who are no longer considered to be in their “prime”. But there is also a whole imaginative dimension evoked by the idea of the lake: water that does not flow, yet is by no means devoid of movement. It struck us as an effective way to describe “Ora sono un lago”, which has various depths, undercurrents, moments of pure light and darkness, murky episodes. And then there is the first line of Sylvia Plath’s poem “Mirror”: ‘I am silvery and exact. I have no preconceptions’, which struck me for its incredible evocative power and seemed to address us and speak for us. Compared to Suono in un tempo trasfigurato, this record feels broader in scope, moving between kosmische electronics, progressive rock, minimalism, soundtrack music, and folk-inflected textures. Did you consciously set out to expand your sonic palette, or did these different musical languages emerge naturally during the writing process? Vittoria: I think the answer is both. It was a conscious process, in the sense that we spent a lot of time talking, reflecting, and thinking about where we wanted to go with this record. At the same time, it felt very natural because the songs developed slowly, with new ideas emerging throughout the process. The material came from many different sources: improvisations in the rehearsal room, patterns that Francesca had recorded on her own and “forgotten” on her computer, and even ideas that emerged in the studio while we were recording the album. When we made the first record, we decided to record essentially the same parts that we played live, without adding many extra instruments, apart from some occasional percussion, piano, or electric guitar to add colour. For this album, we agreed that we wanted to expand our musical world without worrying about how the songs would work on stage or how many instruments we could realistically play as a duo. That gave us the freedom to explore a wider range of atmospheres, powerful and intense at times, but also dreamy, delicate, and sweet. As a result, the songs became more layered and more articulated. In a way, I think we were searching for a sense of freedom, despite the fact that we are still just two people making music together. Several tracks evoke a strong cinematic quality. The opening piece, for example, feels almost like the theme to a lost 1970s Italian independent film, while pieces such as “Acrobata” and “Prove d’esistenza/Il gesto” carry an atmosphere that recalls Carpenter soundtracks, library music, and electronic noir. How important is cinema—or cinematic thinking—to your compositional process? Francesca: Personally, I tend to visualize music through images, and I love cinema and soundtracks, so I like to think that when someone listens to our music, they can create their own very personal movie in their head. I want every song to evoke a mental space, to allow the listener a moment of emotional release. When I was a child, though I had no idea what a soundtrack was, I remember being obsessed with the music of many films and composers, especially Wendy Carlos’s groundbreaking synthesized adaptations of classical music in A Clockwork Orange and the electronic score for The Shining, as well as Maestro Morricone’s lush compositions, of course (I love The Bird with the Crystal Plumage). Carpenter is one of the greatest, too, what I really like is his minimalist approach – achieving maximum effect with simple means – which is a bit of our motto. As for contemporary stuff, I absolutely love Hildur Guðnadóttir’s work, and Mica Levi’s, to name a few. On that note, it’s certainly no secret that both Vittoria and I would love to score music for films. Somehow we already do it – without movies. “Prove d’esistenza/Il gesto” was the first piece in which Francesca experimented with the Moog Mother-32. What did that instrument open up creatively, and how did its possibilities interact with Vittoria’s highly physical and distinctive drumming? Francesca: Our first album was composed using only acoustic drums and a Roland JUNO-60 but for the new record we wanted to expand our palette, and it all happened very naturally when a mutual friend, sound designer Massimo Carozzi, showed me his Moog Mother-32 and lent it to me. I immediately felt a connection with the machine; I started improvising and recording the more textured passages to share them with Vittoria and I loved the raw sound I could come up with. I envisioned this synergy between her distinctive drumming and certain obsessive patterns, and that’s how we wrote songs like “Acrobata” or “Prove d’esistenza/Il gesto”. It’s an instrument I’m still getting to know, unlike the Juno 60, which I’ve owned for about 15 years (though I’m still exploring its full expressive potential). Generally speaking, I need to work with just a few instruments at a time and get a feel for each one. It can take me years. And that’s fine with me. The album seems to balance opposites: intimacy and distance, acoustic and electronic sound, human voices and machine-like rhythms. Tracks such as “Come un riflesso” even suggest a dialogue between progressive rock traditions and more contemporary electronic forms. How do you negotiate these contrasts when composing together? Vittoria: The contrast between acoustic and electronic elements comes quite naturally from the different musical worlds our instruments belong to. Even though Francesca knows the language of rock music very well, in this duo she mostly plays synthesizers and electronic instruments. Our process sometimes begins with improvisation: we play together until we find a cell, a pattern, or an interaction that feels interesting enough to develop into a composition. “Come un riflesso” is a good example of this approach. The track originated from an improvisation in the studio while we were recording the album. Francesco Donadello, our producer, added a tape delay to my drums, and I was hearing both the acoustic drum sound and the delayed signal in my headphones as I played. It felt almost like a conversation between me and the machine, between a physical gesture and its transformed reflection. Later, Francesca added those strange, alienated voices that I love so much, creating yet another layer of dialogue within the piece. In the end, the song became a meeting point between different worlds, acoustic and electronic, human and mechanical, spontaneous and manipulated. Rather than choosing one or the other, we’re interested in the space where these elements overlap and generate something unexpected. The closing sequence—particularly “Oltre le palpebre” and “Lonely Blue Star”—has a very different emotional character from the darker, more tense material earlier in the album. The image of the “lonely blue star” itself is fascinating: a rare celestial object that somehow survives beyond its expected lifespan. What significance does that image hold for you, and did you conceive the album as moving toward a particular emotional or narrative resolution? Francesca: I believe we had a clearer idea of the kind of narrative resolution we wanted to achieve as we were progressing the recordings of the tracks. We recorded more material than what eventually made it to the final version, and one thing we were quite sure about was that the title track would serve as the album’s opening track and “Lonely Blue Star” the closing chapter. It’s about something that can be a long way away and still remain visible, like a star in the sky. From the lake (that can also be a metaphor for our own boundaries, imposed or self-imposed) we wanted to look up. All stars go through life cycles, as we do. It’s all about transcendence, malancholy and mystey. Music as a spiritual quest. Vittoria: Yes, the last two tracks are intended to conclude the record in a peaceful and calmer way. Especially in “Lonely blue star” I can feel this kind of abandon, when the rhythmic drum pattern stops and leaves musical space for more percussive and distended drums, melancholic lines of synth and classical guitar. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — For its third act, PANCAKE underwent a complete makeover once again although band member andguitarist Walter Negele managed to at least retain one member with drummer Hans Derer stickingaround for the band's final release NO ILLUSIONS which came out in 1979. With a new cast ofkeyboardist Uli Frank, bassist Ralf Scheibe and female vocalist Biggi Zmierczak, the band droppedthe Gentle Giant meets Pink Floyd proclivities of "Out Of The Ashes" and focused more on a proggystyle of heavier rock not unlike early Frumpy or other similar German acts such as Night Sun,Message, Birth Control or Murphy's Blend. While the band's first two releases were rather lazy andchilled out, NO ILLUSIONS finally steps things up a bit without jettisoning some of the spacey Eloystyle keyboard effects.An even more forgotten album than the band's earlier offerings, NO ILLUSIONS suffers from much ofthe same lack of inspiration that the band has always faced no matter how many times Negele pickedup the pieces and tried to persevere through. An admirable mix of keyboard intensity woven intoheavier guitar riffs and soaring emotive guitar sweeps that are clearly inspired by Steve Hackettand the early neo-prog style. In some ways this version of PANCAKE sounds a bit like Anyone'sDaughter, the band which swapped drummers after the debut only PANCAKE lacks the same creative edge.The original album featured six tracks in the 40-minute range however newer release feature an equalplaying time of bonus tracks which includes unreleased material and live tracks.Once again this album was lumped into the Krautrock scene but honestly this band never really fitinto that sector of the German prog scene. NO ILLUSIONS is by far the most consistent album of theband's three album run but once again suffers from lackluster songwriting, rather aimlesscompositional developments and never really delivers the goods that take you where you really wantto go. It's the kind of album that teases and then drops the ball, the worst kind however once againnothing is overtly unlistenable. The melodies are pleasant enough and Zmierczak delivers a nicefemale fronted performance on the tracks which is a step up from the previous album. The Eloy-esquekeyboard tricks are also quite nicely incorporated into the rock mix but despite the flawlessintegration the overall compositional flow seems rather tame. Amazingly enough the track "Tears OfTime" reminds me of early Asia.It seemed that the album title signified that Negele was done riding the PANCAKE bandwagon and hadNO ILLUSIONS about spinning his wheels for another fruitless endeavor. Dripping with potential andlost opportunities, NO ILLUSIONS continues the trend of a band that just couldn't get over the humpto take things to the next level. It's admirable that PANCAKE managed to stick it out for a threealbum run when so many superior acts only managed to squeeze out a sole release however in this casethe band was starting to sound too commercial for the prog world and not accessible enough for thebooming new wave and AOR rock scene. It's an OK album but in the sea of excellence that dominatedthe 70s hardly an essential listening experience. Add to that yet another horrifying album cover andit was time to call it a day. I'm still waiting for a compilation titled "House of Pancakes" but sofar no such thing.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — After a major implosion after the poorly received debut album "Roxy Elephant," the German bandPANCAKE returned for its sophomore release aptly titled OUT OF THE ASHES with only guitarist WalterNegele remaining thus forming a completely new band in the process. The new cast members for thisdance of the griddlecakes also included Peter Indrak (bass, violin), Hans Derer (drums), Rainer R�hm(lead vocals, percussion) and at long last a keyboardist with Heinz Bertsch performing on Hammondorgan, clavinet, Fender Rhodes and grand piano. The band completely transmogrified from a WishboneAsh replica style twin guitar pseudo-prog act with no keyboards to a fully engaged dabbler in theart of symphonic prog. OUT OF THE ASHES sounded absolutely nothing like its predecessor and tookcues from English acts such as Gentle Giant and Yes as well as German contemporaries likeGrobschniit and Eloy. Only the space rock of Pink Floyd was retained in the transition.The band immediately declares its new direction with the opening "Painted Rush-Hour" which instantlyevokes the worship of one of England's prog royalty acts, namely Gentle Giant with a funky keyboardgroove that would fit right on home on albums such as "Free Hand" or "The Power And The Glory" andwould be reimplemented throughout the album with moments of the four-part "Rainbow Suite" soundinguncomfortably too close to the original source with even the vocal performances being a dead ringerfor the Schulman brothers distinct lyrical delivery. Likewise other GG-isms are ubiquitouslyseasoned throughout ranging from the contrapuntal elegance that GG excelled at as well as the otherpeculiarities that the band exhibited. "Cakey Funk" dabbles in the prog funk style even further.This album basically featured two lengthy suites bookmarked by two shorter tracks and anotherinserted in between. While the debut barely qualified as prog at all, the band left no ambiguitieson album #2 and went for the prog jugular which unfortunately feels a bit forced, stilted anddisingenuous as the band was trying too hard to emulate rather than create.The album is an oddmishmash of Gentle Giant, Yes, Eloy and the hippie hippie idealisms that gave early Yes releasestheir charm. Despite the album emerging in the late prog year of 1977, the album sounds as if itshould've been inserted into the 1973-74 timeline at the tale end of the initial prog boom. As withthe debut, OUT OF THE ASHES remains a rather low energy affair with the band members rarely breakinginto faster tempos and instead rely on instrumental lallygagging about yet despite the low burningtime extension tactics the album barely misses the 33 minute playing time.Overall it's a pleasant listening experience and one that won't offend but at this point Negeleseemed unsure where to take the band in order to be relevant on the crowded playing field of late tothe prog party acts such as PANCAKE. The main problem with this album is it is grasping at too manystraws and really not achieving anything particularly interesting or innovative. The band hints atturning up the steam into something more profound but always drops the ball before such climacticresolutions manifest. At this point in the band's game it's understandable why this band has beenfairly overlooked over the years since it was very much a second tier band in playing style thatnever brought anything new to the prog table. Add to that the production is a bit lackluster and thevocalist is noticeably weaker than the previous one. Once again there's nothing unlistenable on OUTOF THE ASHES but it's clear this band just never delivered the chops to crank out a totallysatisfying prog experience.

items.body: Review by Matti — In 2013 I was fortunate to discover this German prog band as a reviewer for the Finnish prog magazine Colossus. Their two first albums, Adonis (1979) and Anyone's Daughter (1980) were sung in English, but after the succesful release of Piktors Verwardlungen (1981), the instrumentally oriented, narrated work (based on Hermann Hesse's story of the same name) that had been composed long before the debut, the band decided to continue with their native tongue. In Blau is perhaps their strongest album, a fresh and vital example of light prog of the early 80's. Perhaps the band's sound was also improved by a change of a drummer. Even some Fusion flavour is to be sensed. I believe Barclay James Harvest, which at the time were more popular in Germany than in England, were influental to their accessible and melodic style & sound. But there's more of progressive elements in both the compositions and the arrangements than in the post-Wolstenholme era BJH. Plus the whole album containing seven tracks is surprisingly good from start to finish, despite approaching more typical pop. The slowly growing and grandiose opener wouldn't be difficult to imagine being BJH if it was sung in English. The next piece sonically centres on acoustic guitar reminiscent of Anthony Phillips. The vocals are fairly good even with a slight Eloy vibe in the voice. 'Nichts fur mich' at first sounds like a mediocre non-prog New Wave pop song with its sharp synths, until it turns into instrumentally emphasized piece with a diverse and vintage keyboard arsenal and complexity in rhythm. 'Nach diesem Tag' is for the most part not so far from an 80's pop ballad and yet it isn't a total letdown for prog ears. Somehow I'm thinking of Pendragon c. 1991. 'La La' has only repetition of those syllables amidst instrumental prog. 'Sonne' brings back the Ant Phillips style acoustic guitar. Again the general tempo and atmosphere are rather peaceful, without feeling dull or weak at all. The prog highlight is the 15-minute, three-part 'Tanz un Tod'. The catchy middle section has some resemblance of Asia's debut album, and the slowly built climax starts with an elegant piano solo.The 70's prog tradition and the early 80's prog-rooted pop are friendly shaking hands in this excellently produced album.

items.body: Review by Sean Trane — Well, going through my 90's CD acquisition, I was relistening to NARAJAMA's Vytancuj Chmury, and I realized I never shared my thoughts about it on this site. TBH, I had no idea that they released three or four albums in the XXIst C (with a smaller line-up), but back then, I was highly impressed with "the scene", since I was also into Vyber and Uz Jsme Doma, though Nara was relatively different in terms of Avant-prog, as they're much more accessible. This is their first officially released album, but it was first on a private cassette, and the septet is high on its wheels, especially with their super funky bassist Igor Judas can make you think of RHCP's Flea, just to name one. One might also think of a softer edged Joly Joker's type of funk-metal - Czech band of the 90's barely ever mentioned anywhere). Mihal Mical's vocals are in Czech, but the texts are translated in English in the booklet. Jumpy, quirky, technical and yet, one can imagine also a certain Zappa spirit in the sense of Zolo music, but with a distinct Slavic spirit.The album's booklet is graced with a cute artwork, but the tracks are not presented in the right order and not even numbered, except on the back panel, though there no guarantee either. Overall, one fun album to listen to and revisit every four or five years or so.

items.body: Review by WaldoJeffers — As someone who really enjoys Conrad Schnitzler's early work with Kluster, Tangerine Dream and also solo, I consider "Gold" to be a highly convincing album, standing in the tradition of "Blau" and certainly "Rot", dating from the same creative period as this belatedly released album.Schnitzler experiments here once again with all sorts of electronically generated instruments; briefly, I even hear an accordion. You will search in vain for rhythms and harmonies here, of course; "Gold" is an album of free form. It chirps, pings and creaks merrily away; only in track 12 ? the tracks have no titles ? does something almost akin to a dance mood arise as a result of the electronic percussion; although even to this you can hardly dance, there is simply too much going on. An oriental-sounding flute improvises over heavy chirping and bubbling above the quasi-soloing percussion. Space techno? With the following track, "13", which sounds like a cool, empty factory hall turned into music, a bit of Industrial also comes into play."Gold" is fun and enormously entertaining for those people who (like me) find many of the productions of the "Berlin School" incredibly boring. Not a typical Conrad Schnitzler album, but for me (perhaps for that very reason) one of the best.

items.body: Review by siLLy puPPy — A super rare band from the 1970s German progressive scene which apparently had an affinity for oneof the world's most treasured griddle flapjacks, PANCAKE may have been a strange name for a progband but unlike many obscurities that barely squeaked out a mere album, this band from Winnendenjust north of Stuttgart managed to record three albums with substantial lineup and subsequent stylechanges on each release. The peculiar moniker devolved from the more heady sounding Nyrvana Pancakewhich formed in 1970 and then dropped the mystical part leaving just PANCAKE. Oh i know, what ahorrible name for a prog act which is why i've avoided this band for so long but after findingdipping into this PANCAKE's earliest album, it's surprisingly not as bad as historians seem to makeit out to be.Firstly this band gets unfairly lumped into the Krautrock scene but at this stage the band wasclearly more of a prog related act sounding similar to Wishbone Ash or other twin guitar sensationsfrom the heavy end of the psychedelic spectrum that graced the latter half of the 60s and continuedthroughout the following decade. The debut ROXY ELEPHANT was released in 1975 and was somewhat of afish out of water which is most likely why this band has been relegated to the forgotten pile and itcertainly doesn't help that the album cover depicts a rather pathetic looking circus-abused elephantthat perhaps that may have been rescued by members of Roxy Music hence the puzzling album title?It's a peculiar band and album for sure but the music contained on this debut is far fromunlistenable. In fact it's very pleasant prog-tinged twin guitar rock with a competent vocalist anddecently construed compositions. The band at this point consisted of lead vocalist Hampy Nerlich, guitarists Walter Negele and TommyMetzger / Newton, bassist Werner Bauer and drummer G�nther Konopik. Nyrvana Pancake started out as apsychedelic rock act and those freaky vibes certainly have been retained on ROXY ELEPHANT althoughthe musical style is more akin to British rock with moments of extended passages, time signaturedeviations and crafty prog workouts that don't slap you in the face but rather slowly slink in andout of existence. The music is touted as hard rock but the majority of the album beginning with theopening "Heartfire" features more chill out moments in the space rock mode along with Teutonic folkmelodic embellishments offering a bizarre style that sort of incorporations Wishbone Ash's playingstyle into a Pink Floyd type of space rock only fortified with a medieval sounding tribute to folkmusic. The band is most famous for swapping drummers with Anyone's Daughter after this release.The rock style is more on the bluesy side jumping from various inspirations ranging from not onlyWishbone Ash but also sounds that remind of Electric Sandwich as well as Birth Control and otherheavier German proggers of the day only PANCAKE featured no keyboards and wielded their spaceeffects through the twin guitar and bass motifs. Overall the band was quite skilled with tight knittracks and an above average lead singer despite the slight accent. I wouldn't call PANCAKE's debutrelease one of the most essential releases of the scene but neither is it the avoid-it-at-all-coststype of release that many have lambasted it as. For those who have always hoped for a more spacerock oriented version of Wishbone Ash then this is the band for you, well at least on this firstoffering as the band would shift gears and go more the direction of fellow German proggersGrobschnitt and Eloy. Perhaps this is too mellow and too uninspiring for many but i personally findit quite pleasant.3.5 but the tracks aren't strong enough to round up

items.body: Review by tszirmay — The advantages of having a hardcore attitude towards finding hidden prog gems, especially the more recent ones, is that it requires research on a wide variety of platforms, which can include the obvious internet (or the "Internment net " as I like to call it) but also radio programs and magazines. One can have the best radar in the world but if something flies 10 feet off the ground, you will not see the blip on any screen. Kopilott is from Spain, I have no info on the musicians, even though I did find it on Bandcamp, so for now, we have to live with the artistic anonymity (you won the WC, you can open up now, hombre!). First of all, a stunning cover always help us older fans, as we lived in a time when the artwork was highly indicative of the musical trip within (hello Roger Dean and Hipgnosis, among many others). It pretty much clarifies the sounds provided, a synthesizer-rich aural ocean that seduces , cosmic guitar tributaries that owe to both Steve Hillage or Manuel Gottsching , vivid bass promenades, and a propellant percussive drive which may or may not be organic, all fitting into well-structured either mid-sized or marathon jam sessions.Within seconds of tumbling into "Void", my weary mind had left the sordid negativity of our current miasmic world, immediately strapped into some hurtling space shuttle, taking me and my pointed ears to boldly go where a few may have travelled before (the Federation notwithstanding) and luxuriate in the fulminating journey ahead. I knew right away that I will love this.If one was satisfied visiting the black hole, well hungering for the epic "Lust " may become an obsession, a relentless drum assault bass guitar battery that would make cosmic sex an addiction. A 10 minute + dive-bombing excursion into the vast unknown, where primal functions rule, animal urges deciding which course to take, and orgasmic flow seems the goal of the entire seduction. The use of various effect pedals only adds to the hunger, the pace never abating the slightest bit, just pounding along like a stud. The titillating synths provide all the aural caresses one could ever hope for, only to get rebooted by that lewd bass line. Incredible. The shortest track , a bit over 4 minutes, "Nebula" clouds the issue, coming across as something the venerable Bill Nelson would have composed in the early 2000, and oblique, concrete and staunch romp, the melodious guitar heavily effect-laden, the swarming keys and a bass synth showing little remorse. The buzzing electronics take it in another thunderous direction altogether. "Mirrors" expands on the exuberance, reflecting an almost hypnotic, slowly building JM Jarre feel, before the electric guitar decides to streak into almost forbidden zones, a simply astounding showcase of technical talent, moody atmosphere and compositional excellence. When warp speed seven is attained, hold on to your phasers and strap yourself in? A beeline into delirium, an unforgiving and ruthless onslaught that crosses through a galactic belt, arriving on the other side with only floating intentions of serenity. "Gorgona" opts for a neo-funky tradition, a stringent groove on which the serpentine electric guitar coils rapturously, its gruff texture a hugely attractive appeal. A vocal effect adds all the additional drama one would require, the shimmering keyboard underlay doing its share of theatrics. The stop and start sequence reboots the piece into a darker vein, as if a scene from some lurid sci-fi movie required it as a soundtrack. A beautiful melody can be considered as a "Cursed Delight", and the artist wisely selected a different tack to express himself, in a neo-classical arrangement where tempered stylistics so that the main melody can really stand out. Even the guitar tone is closer to Hackett or Mike Holmes, not exactly paupers. The flute effects and leisurely pastoral feel comes totally unexpected, a most welcome moment on the recording. To finish off with a tremendous rendition of one of the all-time classics (and rarely done successfully with the exception of a few Carlos Santana versions with guest guitarists) "Maggot Brain " is that famous 1970 Funkadelic track where George Clinton told axeman Eddie Hazel to play like if his mother had died. Arguably one of the greatest audio experiences even Jimi (RIP) could ever hope for. The version here is respectfully not a clone but a sensible variation that pays reverence to the original. Cleaner perhaps (lesser use of wah-wah) but just as intense. The addition of keyboards is simply genius, and the final flurry is celestial jubilation incarnate. A wonderfully attractive, fresh, crisp and exciting selection of pieces that bodes very well for having a much larger audience. I enjoyed this immediately and will many more times, I am sure. I also purchased their preceding and following albums.4.5 Navigators

items.body: “Talk about the blood.” Aja Monet says it again and again on “for the Congo,” and by the end you can’t unhear it. The blood is coltan, the metal torn out of the Congo to feed the phone in your hand and the car in your drive, and the war that keeps it coming. The AI boom is hungry for more, and the body count climbs to match. She calls the phones “the death machines in our palms,” and yes, she means the one you’re reading this on. The percussion is heavy and the ground keeps moving under her, and she rides it, picking up speed as the names stack up: Paul Kagame, cosy with the West, then the World Bank, the IMF, everyone with a hand in the till. She’s a surrealist blues poet by trade, but she’s said this one cuts too close to dress up, so she doesn’t. She lays it out and dares you to look away. The poem started at a march in the UK in 2024, when a woman beside her shouted about the blood on the phone in her hand. That shout became this. It’s the sixth track on the color of rain, her second album after 2023’s when the poems do what they do, made with Meshell Ndegeocello and Justin Brown, out 22 May on drink sum wtr. The video opens on Michel Kuka Mboladinga, the DR Congo supporter known as Lumumba Vea, and Monet has said his image brought her to tears. He spends entire matches standing frozen on a pedestal, one arm raised, dressed as Patrice Lumumba, the country’s first prime minister, murdered in 1961 by a firing squad with Belgian and CIA hands on it, then dismembered and dissolved in acid so there’d be no grave. Everyone around him sings and leaps; he holds still, a living statue keeping a dead man in the room. items.body: This three-CD box set is something of a rarity, given that many of Jorge Bolet‘s live performances recorded professionally have not been released commercially. The two Ambassador Auditorium recitals (1981 and 1986) are from the last decade of an illustrious career. Originally intended as archival recordings, they have been restored and remastered to give us a chance to hear Bolet in the space he preferred — the stage. Ambassador Recitals Amazon Presto Apple Schumann’s Op. 17 Fantasy is one of the major works in the November 11, 1981 performance. Compared to more contemplative recordings (Richter and Perahia come to mind), this version leans toward extroversion, an interesting dynamic to bring to a work that is introspective at its core. The opening lines of the first movement (CD 1, track 4) feature emphatic dotted rhythms and chords that feel a bit punchy. Taken in the larger context of the movement’s yearning, however, Bolet’s interpretation makes total sense. He captures the passionate spirit and communicates its rawness. At the same time, he connects with the audience on a deeper level in quieter moments, like the hymn-like material at 5’00”. Bolet’s joyous energy in the middle movement is enough to uplift the most discerning listener, wrong notes and all, but the most convincing movement is the Langsam (CD 1, track 6). The pace is more measured than Pollini or Argerich, yet perfectly suits the transcendent nature of the writing. While Pollini’s version is memorable for its tonal beauty, Bolet’s stands out for the flexibility he brings to the phrasing; the small pauses at choice moments add to the expressivity of the lines. The 1981 concert features a selection of Schubert-Liszt song transcriptions, of which Der Müller und der Bach (CD 1, track 8) stands out as a study in nuance. Beyond the impeccable voice leading, the melody takes on a distinctly vocal quality, the pianist showing a clear understanding of how the voice inflects and moves and, most importantly, expresses grief and loss. The famous Erlkönig (CD 1, track 11) is a completely different take from the benchmark live recording of Evgeny Kissin’s 1990 Carnegie Hall debut. Where Kissin fuels the drama and terror through speedy, aggressive octaves, Bolet establishes a more austere presence. His reading of the character of Death speaks to inevitability rather than urgency, yet is no less frightening. A Unified Theme of Ballades The repertoire of the 1986 recital is thoughtfully curated: Grieg’s Op. 24 Ballade, Brahms’s Op. 10 Ballades, and Liszt’s S. 171 Ballade are works that have received less exposure, complementing Chopin‘s more famous cycle. In the Grieg, Bolet captures the tonal ambiguity that seems to set up the eclectic, unpredictable spirit of the whole work. Lyricism, whimsy, and cataclysm are all rendered with conviction, yet Bolet ties them together with a unified sense of sadness. While Brahms’s early Op. 10 set lacks the profundity of the late Op. 116–119, the seeds of that language are already present. In No. 1, Bolet evokes the tension between subtlety and storminess through rapid surges from soft to loud, lending persistence to the recurring four-note motif. No. 2 offers a similarly effective juxtaposition of opposites, though at times the loud passages come off too strident. No. 3 has the most striking personality, its off-kilter melodic material giving Bolet room to build an inviting unpredictability. For all its raging fury, the latter part of the Intermezzo reveals some of his most tender playing of the program. Jorge Bolet, Paris, 1988. Photo © Wilhelm Fröling. As the centerpiece of the 1986 recital, the four Chopin Ballades (CD 3, tracks 2–5) don’t disappoint. The most striking aspect throughout is Bolet’s game of opposites. In the F major Ballade, grace and fury interplay dramatically; the minor sections are especially memorable as they edge on a recklessness that rarely surfaces in his normally deliberate style. As the most difficult and perhaps most emotionally complex of the set, the final Op. 52 is beautifully rendered and shows years of familiarity with the work. The F minor sections, despite their melancholy, reveal his sensitivity to Chopin’s shifts in harmonic color, and the lithe melodic lines capture the essence of bel canto. The Coda is one of the most electric moments of the recital. Given that the concerts were originally recorded on open-reel tapes, the 24-bit/96 kHz transfer and remastering by Kabir Hermon and John Croft is impressive. The fidelity of Bolet’s playing comes across cleanly, as does the character of the instrument. Hearing archival recordings with this much clarity is a rare pleasure, especially from a legend of the twentieth century. items.body: I wasn’t really looking for death I was just looking for myself Six months after the release of Christine Plays Viola’s 2026 album F.I.V.E. (Fear Increases Violent Emotions), the Italian darkwave and post-punk band returns to complete its story. Their latest single “At Last, I Found You” was recorded during the album sessions but deliberately held back, allowing the record’s emotional course to reach listeners before its final companion piece appeared. “At Last, I Found You” begins with synthesizers sighing like brakes slowing a car on a wet road. A low drone hangs behind them until the bass establishes forward momentum, the drums lock into place, and an insistent guitar hook cuts through the gathering pressure. The song soon settles into the kind of danceable gothic rock Christine Plays Viola handle so well: immediate enough for the club, yet weighted with genuine psychic anguish. During the verses, the instruments pull back around the dark, smoldering vocal while bass and drums continue to propel the song beneath faint synthesizers. When the refrain of “break me up, break me up” takes hold, the arrangement surges upward. The guitars broaden, the rhythm bears down, and the vocal rises from exhausted confession into a passionate cry. Direct, memorable, and emotionally severe, it stands among the band’s finest songs to date. The song describes the urge to drive away as an act of self-erasure. After burying the keys to a box containing his dreams, vocalist Massimo Ciampani sings of driving into the night, although he is already convinced that some part of him has died. Cigarette ash, blood, chains, a ditch, and the void surround a man who can no longer recognize himself. Yet the apparent second person referred to in the title gradually assumes another identity. The “you” he has been seeking is his childhood self: the innocence and possibility he abandoned somewhere along the way. The final admission—“I wasn’t really looking for death, I was just looking for myself”—recasts the song’s death drive as a desperate attempt at psychological recovery. By restoring the album’s full title in parentheses, “At Last, I Found You” brings the F.I.V.E. cycle back to its central concern: the point at which fear turns inward, distorts emotion, and threatens to destroy the person carrying it. Guitarist and bandleader Fabrizio Giampietro explains: “At Last, I Found You was always the most immediate and instinctive song we wrote during the F.I.V.E. sessions. We deliberately left it off the album because we wanted listeners to experience that record’s emotional arc without this song becoming its centre of gravity. Six months later, it felt like the right moment to finally share it.” The accompanying video transfers that crisis to a rain-swept nocturnal drive. A leather-jacketed man grips the steering wheel as vacant commercial streets pass beneath violet, red, and electric-blue light. Rain crowds the windows, cigarette smoke fills the cabin, and the camera repeatedly glances toward the empty back seat, leaving a conspicuous space for the person invoked by the song’s title. As the drive continues, the city begins losing its physical certainty. Light bends across the windshield, the road appears to warp, and black mist gathers around the car as the driver’s composure gives way to panic. His gestures become increasingly frantic while flashes of red and blue appear through the rain, suggesting either an approaching police confrontation or another fragment of his unraveling mind. After stopping the car, he steps into the downpour and finds a boy in a blue raincoat waiting across the road. The child stands motionless, staring back at him with an expression that offers neither recognition nor judgment. It is the video’s clearest answer to the lyrics, yet the encounter never establishes whether the boy is a memory, a hallucination, a chance at salvation, or an image seen at the instant of death. The street empties once again, and an overhead view shows the black mist closing around the abandoned car. The video then returns to the back seat, where a small toy car rests beneath the closing credits—the only physical trace of the childhood the driver has spent the night pursuing. He may have found the boy, but finding him and saving him remain two different acts. Watch the video for “At Last, I Found You” below: “At Last, I Found You (Fear Increases Violent Emotions)” is out now through Bandcamp, Spotify, and all major digital platforms. Christine Plays Viola will continue supporting F.I.V.E. with European appearances running from August through October, including dates in Poland, Spain, England, and Germany. Further performances are currently being confirmed. items.body: Release me from this curse- let my blood flow As above, we will meet below Casting a midnight shadow, Bleached Cross opens up their latest single, Blood Moon, with guitars that seem to hang above the song like pale fire, while the drums advance at a funereal pace and the synthesizers spread a cold, metallic glow. The final preview of Wrath, due July 24 through New Morality Zine, finds the Chicago band stretching dark wave toward blackened grandeur without losing the pull of a huge chorus. Every part leans toward catastrophe, yet the song keeps one hand firmly around a love story. Lyrically, the song traverses fallen kingdoms, fields of impaled bodies, and a private apocalypse populated by obedient demons. Its vampiric imagery carries a conspicuous echo of Francis Ford Coppola’s Bram Stoker’s Dracula: a bereaved lover who feels betrayed by God, moves through the remains of Vlad the Impaler’s cruelty, hungers for blood beneath a crimson moon, and vows to find the beloved in any lifetime. The connection lies more closely with Coppola’s romantic reinvention than with Stoker’s original novel, as grief becomes damnation and desire reaches across centuries in search of reunion. Blood, sacrifice, and eternal return crowd the verses, but Bleached Cross never allows the imagery to collapse into decorative horror. The violence springs from devotion warped beyond reason. Love has outlived the beloved, leaving behind something feral, blasphemous, and prepared to cross any border that death tries to enforce. “This song is about eternal love, devotion, and the idea of fate bonding people together even beyond death, as love is the one thing death is unable to take away from the living,” says the band. “The ending implies the taking of someone else’s life to ease their suffering, knowing fate will bind you together again in the next life, but it can also be interpreted as killing yourself to be with someone who has passed…both ideas come up in other songs on the album.” That final ambiguity cuts straight through the song’s gothic romance. Mercy and murder begin to resemble one another; suicide appears as both surrender and reunion. The guitars climb in patient layers, the rhythm section keeps the procession moving, and the synthesizers thicken the air until the closing passage surges outward in a blast of melody and ruin. The song’s last ascent offers no clean resolution. Instead, Bleached Cross leave the listener inside the vow itself, where love survives by becoming monstrous enough to follow the dead through every kingdom, lifetime, grave, and promised return. Like Dracula mistaking damnation for fidelity, the song makes eternal love inseparable from the curse that sustains it. Listen below: Formed remotely in 2019 by Zak and Alex, Bleached Cross grew from a file-sharing project between Chicago and San Diego into a full live band. Their early demos, split with Shamewave, 2022 self-titled LP, and 2024 collaboration with The True Faith gradually fused post-punk, industrial music, blackened hardcore, and noise rock into a severe but flexible language. Blood Moon shows the band handling that language with new confidence. Recorded with Andy Nelson at Bricktop Recording during 2025, Wrath circles grief, guilt, death, and redemption across ten tracks. Here, those concerns become a feverish vampiric romance, full of crimson mountains, impaled bodies, infernal vows, and impossible loyalty. Listen to Blood Moon below, and order Wrath here. Wrath by Bleached Cross Next month, Bleached Cross will team up with Milwaukee screamo band snag for a tour across the U.S. that begins August 4 in Indianapolis, IN, at Healer. items.body: Boy Harsher have announced Get Mean, their first new album since the 2022 film and soundtrack The Runner. Due September 18 via Atlantic Records, the twelve-track album follows Jae Matthews and Augustus Muller through the breakup of their romantic relationship, a period of familial loss and creative uncertainty, and the difficult decision to continue Boy Harsher together. Alongside the announcement, the duo have unveiled “Hard Beat,” a lean, driving darkwave track accompanied by a Boy Harsher-directed video about surveillance, deviance, desire, and trauma. Where June’s “Jeans” introduced their return through wiry new wave guitar and western detail, “Hard Beat” bears down on the machinery that first made Boy Harsher such a commanding presence in clubs: a catchy bass-synth figure, an unrelenting kick drum, and Matthews’ voice cutting through the track like cold air rushing through an open car window. One cannot help but hear a trace of Depeche Mode’s “Behind the Wheel” in its fusion of movement, erotic surrender, and mechanical repetition. Boy Harsher pushes that feeling toward a harder, more body-driven strain of darkwave, with the bass carrying the physical weight while Matthews slips between confession, invitation, and command. The highway becomes both an escape route and a place where control can abruptly change hands. Directed by Boy Harsher with cinematography from Owen Smith-Clark, the video draws from Helmut Newton’s 1995 “High and Mighty” feature and the sexually charged queer punk cinema of Gregg Araki. It opens inside a windowless room lined with yellowed tiles, where an old CRT television displays Angel Zinovieff seated in a wheelchair. The image soon cuts from the monitor to Zinovieff herself, dressed in black with one leg held inside an elaborate metal brace. Rods and clamps run along her fishnet-covered limb, turning an orthopedic device into something between medical apparatus, restraint, and severe fetishwear. The camera studies the brace in close-up before moving to the controls of a vintage Cadillac tearing along a nearly deserted highway at night. Metal joints, pedals, switches, leather gloves, and the car’s gear selector enter into a visual correspondence with the hardware fastened around Zinovieff’s leg. The human body and the automobile appear as related machines, each capable of movement while remaining subject to whoever controls its mechanisms. Inside the Cadillac, Cheeky Ma and Mo Stark play the two “freaky deviants” hurtling through the blue-black night. The driver smokes, laughs, paws at the dashboard, and turns a handheld MiniDV camcorder on the other occupants, its mounted light firing directly into their faces. At moments, the camcorder is raised with the casual recklessness of someone filming a party while driving; elsewhere, its bright eye takes on the invasive force of an interrogation lamp. Rings, lacquered nails, facial piercings, glossy fabric, and black leather crowd the frame as passing streetlights sweep across the interior. Jae Matthews occupies the backseat beneath a black funeral veil. Red and green light divide her face behind the netting as she sings directly toward the lens, sometimes alone and sometimes pressed close against another veiled figure. The mesh softens and fractures their features, lending the encounters an uneasy intimacy: a kiss, a threat, and an identification photograph can seem separated by only a few frames. Matthews remains a passenger, yet her fixed gaze and repeated appeals to “make it real” steadily pull the car’s disorder around her. The highway is continually fed back into the tiled room through the CRT monitor. At first, the television shows Zinovieff in her wheelchair; it later carries the empty road, faces from the Cadillac, and camcorder images stamped with a red recording indicator and apparent geographic coordinates. Those transfers make it increasingly difficult to determine who is watching whom. The people in the Cadillac document each other, the closed-circuit system observes the room, and the video finally points its cameras outward at the audience. Under choreography by performance artist Monica Mirabile of FLUCT, Zinovieff’s physical restraint develops into a violent, increasingly expansive dance. She folds at the waist, whips her hair, claws at her clothing, arches backward, and strikes the tiled walls with open palms. Her movements carry the strain of a body fighting both its enclosure and the device attached to it. The editing cuts these gestures against the Cadillac’s acceleration, collapsing stillness and speed into the same state of agitation. Blue highway footage, sickly green tiles, sudden red washes, and overexposed camcorder glare keep the two locations visually connected. As the song intensifies, the cuts become faster and the images less stable: veiled faces double against one another, the driver leans toward the camera with a feral grin, Zinovieff’s hair lashes across her face, and the road stretches ahead without revealing a destination. Near the end, the Cadillac is viewed from outside, with its occupants compressed behind the windshield and Matthews’ veiled face visible within the moving vehicle. The car continues through the darkness as though escape itself has become another form of confinement. The video also sharpens the track’s resemblance to Depeche Mode’s “Behind the Wheel.” Anton Corbijn’s film famously presents Dave Gahan with an injured leg and crutches before a woman assumes control of the journey. “Hard Beat” rearranges that imagery around Zinovieff’s brace, the vintage Cadillac, female control, and the unstable line between passenger and captive. Those shared elements—bodily injury, roadway travel, erotic power, and surrendered agency—make the connection unusually specific, while Boy Harsher drives the idea into a harder and more openly confrontational setting. The MiniDV camcorder establishes another suggestive post-punk reference. Its repeated appearance in “Hard Beat,” together with Nathaniel Jerome’s promotional portrait of Gus Muller pointing a camcorder directly at the viewer while Matthews stands behind him, immediately recalls the artwork and promotional campaign for New Order’s 2001 album Get Ready. Photographed by Jürgen Teller under Peter Saville’s art direction, that campaign similarly placed a handheld camera between its subject and audience. With Boy Harsher calling their album Get Mean, another clipped two-word imperative beginning with “Get,” the parallel feels likely intentional, even though the duo have not explicitly confirmed it. Here, New Order’s invitation to be prepared becomes Boy Harsher’s warning to toughen up. Watch the video for Hard Beat below: Get Mean began during a period when the continuation of Boy Harsher was far from assured. In early 2024, after years of international touring, increasingly ambitious collaborations, and projects that moved between music and film, Matthews and Muller ended their relationship. The separation followed personal turmoil, family loss, and a creative block that left the prospect of another album feeling remote. The situation confronted the pair with questions that reached beyond the ordinary mechanics of making another record: What happens when a band that’s been forged in intimacy, cloaked in the sonic textures of darkly swooning electronics, and dedicated to plumbing the complex and contradictory depths of romantic feeling falls apart? What’s left after grief takes everything? What does a breakup album look like for a band as singular as Boy Harsher? Writing resumed when Matthews took to the road, moving through West Texas, the Pacific Northwest, South Florida, and points between. That unsettled geography became part of the album itself. Described as Boy Harsher’s “road album,” Get Mean was recorded across eight locations in the United States, Mexico, and Italy, gathering cellphone voice notes, environmental fragments, and changing emotional states along the way. Matthews describes the album as: “what I had to give during the most extreme period of my life.” Across its twelve tracks, the familiar coldwave propulsion of Boy Harsher meets detuned pads, squelching synth leads, pedal-steel bends, New Romantic guitar, percussive jokes, and unadorned recordings captured on a phone. Those additions allow grief and exhaustion to coexist with flirtation, humor, and the possibility of beginning again. The record follows the collapse of one form of intimacy while testing whether another—the creative bond between Matthews and Muller—can survive it. Get Mean arrives September 18 via Atlantic Records. Pre-order and pre-save the album here. GET MEAN by Boy Harsher Matthews and Muller formed Boy Harsher in 2014 after meeting while studying film in Savannah. Their first EP, Lesser Man, began as a small cassette release before the track “Pain” spread widely online. The duo followed it with Yr Body Is Nothing in 2016, the Country Girl EP in 2017, and Careful in 2019. Their filmmaking background came fully into view with The Runner, the 2022 horror film and accompanying soundtrack that they wrote, produced, directed, and scored. Their cinematic work continues with The Lonely Woman, their forthcoming feature-length horror thriller starring Chloë Sevigny, FKA twigs, Sturgill Simpson, Will Oldham, and Jake Weary. Boy Harsher are directing the film and providing its score. Following the release of Get Mean, Boy Harsher will begin an extensive North American headline tour before continuing through Europe and the United Kingdom. The itinerary includes sold-out two-night runs in Chicago and Portland, a sold-out Los Angeles appearance at the Hollywood Palladium, and a London headline show at the Roundhouse. items.body: Band: Athak | Album: Primarï | Genre: Zeuhl | Bandcamp Hong Kong-based one-man zeuhl act Athak is back with their latest release. Primarï sees Athak veer into some new territory. Chinese music plays a prominent role, something I had not heard previously from this act. (Maybe they’ve done it before; I don’t know. Athak is quite prolific, and I haven’t heard everything.) “Iyelō” leans into some Canterbury influences, especially Third-era Soft Machine. Yangqin and erhu lend some very unique textural contrasts throughout the album. This record is inspired by colors, and fittingly, the music here embraces the full spectrum. Score: 76/100 Band: Chafouin | Album: Chafouin Orchestra | Genre: Krautrock, Modern classical | Bandcamp Brittany-based experimental math rockers Chafouin are back with a new 26-minute opus. Joining Chafouin on this record is a small orchestra, adding a new layer of depth to their music. The whole ensemble utilizes repetition beautifully, with themes gradually building and slowly morphing. Jagged guitar lines are rounded out with flute, saxophone, and violin, and wordless vocals lend a certain fanciful character. The mood grows noisier and more chaotic as this piece progresses, imbuing it with a sense of constant forward momentum that never feels drawn-out. Score: 91/100 Band: Deathbird Earth | Album: Objective Consciousness | Genre: Space rock, Post-metal | Bandcamp The debut record from Philadelphia’s Deathbird Earth blends eerie, restrained passages led by sci-fi synth tones with heavier moments where elements of noise rock and sludge metal come crashing through. Hypnotic guitar lines channel classic space rock acts like Hawkwind, and other influences are as varied as Neurosis and Devo. The four-part 20-minute conclusion to this record, “Time”, is a powerful storming epic. Score: 78/100 Band: Lunar Shadow | Album: The Pall of a Past World | Genre: Progressive rock, Hard rock | Bandcamp This German band’s newest album is a high-energy bit of proggy, retro-flavored hard rock. The playing is complex and inventive, and it’s clear there’s a lot of enthusiasm behind this music. For me, at least, this unfortunately falls into something of an uncanny valley of retro-rock that I’m simply not a fan of. They haven’t fully embraced retro sounds (like Wobbler or Ring Van Mobius)–which is itself a bit of a risky proposition–but they also haven’t quite gone far enough in infusing more modern sounds (like Zopp or Moura). It’s fine, but this simply isn’t jumping out to me. Score: 72/100 Artist: Bruno Pernadas | Album: unlikely, maybe | Genre: Progressive pop | Bandcamp Portuguese composer and multi-instrumentalist Bruno Pernadas plays a laid-back and light variety of pop music that demonstrates a lot of inventiveness. The mood here is sunny and smooth, and he effortlessly incorporates elements of folk, tropicalia, traditional Portuguese music, and even dashes of hip-hop into a cohesive whole. Textures are lush and smooth, full of silky synthesizers and fluttering flutes. And though psychedelic-tinged pop music is the focus here, there are plenty of jazzy asides and surprising structural switch-ups. Many instrumental tones hearken back to space-age pop and lounge music. This album manages to be both relaxing and deeply engaging, a tough tightrope to walk. Score: 87/100 Band: Telegraph | Album: Topography of Mind | Genre: Progressive rock | Bandcamp The latest release from this Israeli quartet consists of four long pieces, each around 11 minutes long. In it, they cultivate classic space rock and psychedelic textures and pair them with intelligent and creative structural choices. (Pink Floyd is a very, very obvious influence here, with the last couple minutes of this record being borderline-plagiarism of “Shine on You Crazy Diamond”.) The songs evolve in manners which feel natural and help to build senses of drama and weight. The particular tones and textures here are mostly rather light, with a sense of warmth and hopefulness.  Score: 77/100

items.excerpt: Colony 5 member and songwriter Magnus Kalnins releases the third album from his solo project Chaos Tamed, “Nordverk”, via I/O Music on July 24, 2026. The album mixes EBM, IDM and dark electro, described by I/O Music as the project’s “hardest and most concentrated statement yet.” “Nordverk” runs nine tracks: “Determination,” “Core,” “Nightmare,” “Advesaries,” “Destroyer,” “Slaughter,”
items.body: Colony 5 member and songwriter Magnus Kalnins releases the third album from his solo project Chaos Tamed, “Nordverk”, via I/O Music on July 24, 2026. The album mixes EBM, IDM and dark electro, described by I/O Music as the project’s “hardest and most concentrated statement yet.” “Nordverk” runs nine tracks: “Determination,” “Core,” “Nightmare,” “Advesaries,” “Destroyer,” “Slaughter,” “Conflict,” “Sodium” and “The Bells.” Track five, “Destroyer,” was issued in May 2026 as the album’s advance single ahead of the full release. The album is currently available as a digital pre-order on Bandcamp, with the “Destroyer” track streaming now and the complete album unlocking on release day; downloads are offered in MP3, FLAC and 24-bit/48kHz formats. No CD edition has been announced for “Nordverk” so far, unlike Chaos Tamed’s previous two albums, which both had physical releases. Nordverk by Chaos Tamed Chaos Tamed’s ‘Nordverk’ follows 2025’s ‘Elbrus’ Chaos Tamed previously spoke to Side-Line in an interview about the project, which Kalnins has described as more of a laboratory than a conventional band. That conversation followed the release of “Elbrus”, Chaos Tamed’s second album, issued via I/O Music on May 30, 2025 in both digital and CD formats. “Nordverk” is the project’s next full-length since then. About Chaos Tamed Chaos Tamed is the solo project of Magnus Kalnins, a long-standing member and songwriter of Swedish futurepop band Colony 5. The project began as a side venture during a creative hiatus from Colony 5 and has since grown into an independent body of work, moving between EBM, IDM, dark electro and futurepop, built on ethereal, ghostly vocals over pulsing basslines and cinematic textures. The debut Chaos Tamed album, “Shock Waves,” was released via I/O Music on November 9, 2023, and received a nomination for Electronic Album of the Year at the GAFFA Awards in early 2024. The second album, “Elbrus,” followed on I/O Music on May 30, 2025, available digitally and on CD. The advance single “Destroyer” arrived in May 2026, sharpening the project’s harder, more industrial edge ahead of the third album, “Nordverk,” out July 24, 2026 via I/O Music.

items.body: Pittsburgh darkwave and post-punk duo Lowsunday has shared an official video for “You’re So Wired”, the opening track on their “Low Sunday Ghost Machine – Black EP”, released via Projekt Records. The video, directed by Jer Herring, builds its imagery around rapid eye movement footage that mixes dreaming with erratic behavior. Low Sunday Ghost Machine – Black EP by Lowsunday The “Black EP” contains five tracks: “You’re So Wired”, “Shattered”, “Someone To Talk To”, “This Is Not Heaven” and “Don’t Want To Dream Again”. Lyrics are by Shane Sahene, with music written by Sahene and Bobby Spell; the pair also recorded, mixed, mastered and produced the EP themselves. The cover photo is by Shane Sahene, layout is by Christina Sahene, the digital cover edit is by Sam Rosenthal, and band photos are by Christina Sahene. Shane Sahene on the ‘You’re So Wired’ video Shane Sahene explained the idea behind the song and its video: “‘You’re So Wired’ is a song that touches on a manic type of experience. It also touches on the classic Chuang Tzu question, after having had a vivid dream: ‘am I man dreaming I am a butterfly or am I a butterfly dreaming I am a man?’ The experience of not knowing if you’re awake or dreaming. In this case, the rapid eye movements shown in the video capture both dreaming and erratic behavior, making it hard to interpret which is which.” Bobby Spell described how the track sets up the rest of the EP: “Our ‘Black EP’ is deceptive, opening with energetic and wistful ‘You’re So Wired’ but followed by songs that are melancholy and introspective. These are the strongest songs we’ve yet done. With strong and memorable melodies, they invoke feelings of isolation and sadness, but in a way that feels familiar instead of depressing, leaving a sense of hope.” Black EP follows the ‘White EP’ and a shoegaze box-set appearance The “Black EP” is the darker counterpart to Lowsunday’s “Low Sunday Ghost Machine – White EP”, which the band released at the end of 2025 and which ranked second on Post-Punk.com’s Best EPs of 2025. Side-Line covered two further singles from that EP, “Soft Capture” and “Nevver”, alongside the earlier “Innocence (2025 electro mix)” video from the band’s 2025 remaster. Lowsunday’s earlier track “She Follows Rain” also appears on “We Are The Beautiful”, Cherry Red Records’ 4CD box set gathering 67 shoegaze tracks from 1991 to 2011, available via Projekt Records’ Bandcamp store. About Lowsunday Lowsunday formed in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania in 1994 under the name Low Sunday Ghost Machine. The band self-released its debut album, “Low Sunday Ghost Machine”, in 1996, followed by “Elesgiem” in 1999, both through Projekt Records. Both albums were later reissued, with “Low Sunday Ghost Machine” marking its 30th anniversary and “Elesgiem” its 25th. The band disbanded after 1999 and remained inactive for close to 25 years. Lowsunday resurfaced in 2025 as a duo of original members Shane Sahene (vocals, guitar, synth, bass, drums) and Bobby Spell (bass, guitar, drums). Their return produced the “Low Sunday Ghost Machine – White EP” at the end of 2025, followed in 2026 by its darker counterpart, the “Low Sunday Ghost Machine – Black EP”, again via Projekt Records. “You’re So Wired” is the opening track of that Black EP and the subject of the band’s newest video.

items.body: German dark EBM duo Prager Handgriff release the live album “live in Zwickau” on October 30, 2026 through emmobiz records. The label issues the recording as a vinyl LP set with a bonus 7-inch, and separately as a CD box. The album documents Prager Handgriff’s performance at the Elektrisch Festival, held at Club Seilerstraße in Zwickau, on February 28, 2026, in front of a sold-out club. Side-Line has covered the festival’s recent editions, including the 18th Elektrisch Festival and the 19th Elektrisch Festival line-ups. The vinyl set spans ten tracks across two sides: “Tibet,” “Arbeit,” “Schwermetall,” “Klaus” and “Für immer” on side A, and “Schindluder,” “Maschinensturm,” “Traumsequenz,” “Bilder” and “Frontal” on side B. It comes with a bonus 7-inch carrying a one-off live version of “Deutschland” featuring Calva Y Nada. The CD box edition presents the same eleven tracks in sequence, closing with “Deutschland” featuring Calva Y Nada. Order details for both the vinyl set and the CD box are listed on the emmobiz records shop. ‘live in Zwickau’ and Calva Y Nada’s Zwickau live series The pairing with Calva Y Nada on “live in Zwickau” continues a run of Zwickau live recordings on emmobiz records: the label also released Calva Y Nada’s own “El calor de Zwickau”, which likewise carries the joint “Deutschland” performance as bonus material. About Prager Handgriff Prager Handgriff is a German dark EBM project formed in 1990 in Witten by Stefan Schäfer (vocals, electronic drums) and Volker Rathmann (keyboards, programming). The duo used the name “Der Prager Handgriff” for its early work. Their debut album, “Arglistige Täuschung,” was released in April 1993, followed a year later by “Täterschaft & Teilnahme,” which helped establish the project within Germany’s electronic scene. Prager Handgriff released the album “Maschinensturm” via Infacted Recordings in 1995. In 2005 the band issued the best-of double CD “Handarbeiten” as a retrospective, again crediting itself as “Der Prager Handgriff.” The album “Arbeit, Sport und Spiel” followed on Electric Tremor Dessau in 2011, its first release of new material in several years. Prager Handgriff released “Das Letzte Gefecht” via Infacted Recordings in 2022. In 2025, “Arglistige Täuschung” was reissued on vinyl for the first time, on double coloured vinyl with three bonus tracks, through Assur Anshar Records and Rune Serpent Europa. Prager Handgriff’s February 2026 performance at the Elektrisch Festival in Zwickau is now documented on “live in Zwickau,” released via emmobiz records.

items.body: The Autumn Aurora have released “False Idols”, the Italian post-punk and darkwave band’s new single, out now on all major digital platforms through Volcano Records with an accompanying official music video. “False Idols” is the title track of the band’s forthcoming debut album, and follows the debut single “Plastic Altar,” released on June 26, 2026 through the same label. Volcano Records describes “False Idols” as tracing “the loneliness of those confronting a society dominated by propaganda, appearances and false models imposed by politics, religion and mass media,” portraying a reality in which the weakest are crushed rather than protected while false prophets serve the interests of those in power. That same loneliness, per the label, turns into clarity: stepping outside the media spectacle means rediscovering oneself and rejecting a world built on money, easy smiles and illusions. Musically, “False Idols” pushes The Autumn Aurora’s post-punk and darkwave sound to its limits. Synths and analogue orchestral pads intertwine with two electric basses: one builds the groove alongside the drums, while the other takes on a lead-guitar role, using chorus, flanger and delay to shape cold, spectral atmospheres. The label credits the track’s vocals to Saveria Maitilasso, described as “deep and theatrical” – a different name from the vocalist, Vera Perkins, credited on the band’s debut single “Plastic Altar” in June 2026; Side-Line has not been able to confirm whether this reflects a lineup change or a different billing for the same performer. The Autumn Aurora, from ‘Plastic Altar’ to ‘False Idols’ “False Idols” arrives as the second single from The Autumn Aurora, following “Plastic Altar”, which the band released as its debut single on June 26, 2026, also via Volcano Records and also backed by an official video. Both tracks are pulled from the band’s forthcoming debut album, also titled “False Idols.” About The Autumn Aurora The Autumn Aurora is a Rome-based post-punk and darkwave band built around a rare two-bass lineup, with no standard guitar, alongside keyboards and drums. Side-Line previously reported on the band’s debut single “Plastic Altar”, released June 26, 2026 through Volcano Records & Promotion, the Turin-based label, and credited at the time to a lineup of Vera Perkins (vocals), Stefano Ferramola (bass), Francesca Buompane (bass), Chiara Bellucco (drums) and Fabrizio “Nemo” Mancini (keyboards). “Plastic Altar” was recorded, mixed and mastered at GreenMountainAudio Studio with Danilo Silvestri. The band’s forthcoming debut album, “False Idols,” has previously been reported for a September 11, 2026 release on Volcano Records; the label’s new single of the same title is the second piece of music shared from that album. Further band information is available through the group’s Linktree.

items.body: Kyiv-based dark rock and new age band AndrosLand has released a teaser for a new music video, “Душа Лісу” (“The Soul of the Forest”), set to premiere on August 8. The teaser is the band’s first music video activity since 2015. The video was filmed in wintertime Kharkiv, a regional center located roughly 20 kilometers from the border, and produced by the team of Cinemuse.films. Actors Anna Fedorenko and Glib Chaplin filmed the outdoor scenes barefoot in the snow during December 2025, with Chaplin appearing topless in the winter cold. AndrosLand founder Oleg Andros, who has served in the Armed Forces of Ukraine since February 24, 2022, thanked the pair for their “resilience in the name of art.” “Душа Лісу” introduces the Goddess of the Forest, a figure the band describes as bringing human souls into the world, remaining present throughout a person’s life, and guiding them into the afterlife after death. Andros described the song as “new age and rock with a solo on the bagpipe,” crediting bagpiper Anton “Kay” Korolyov for his performance. He added: “We’re waiting for the premiere with bated breath, because AndrosLand hasn’t released a music video in a long time – not since 2015. We put a lot of effort into both the song and the filming.” The track originated as an instrumental with a French title, “Je chanterai juste pour toi,” self-released on an EP in 2015 with French lyrics written by AndrosLand lead vocalist Marina Novikova in 2014-2015. The Ukrainian-language version, “Душа Лісу,” will feature on AndrosLand’s upcoming album, “Hope,” which does not yet have a confirmed release date. Angelina Nepokulchytska provides vocals on “Душа Лісу”; Oleg Andros wrote and composed the track and also performs on it. Vocals were recorded by Pavlo Tymchenko and Nata Sivkova, with guitar, arrangement, recording, mixing and mastering handled by Ivan Luzan at Soncesvit Studio. About AndrosLand AndrosLand was founded in Kyiv in 2011 by Oleg Andros and has released three albums. Side-Line previously covered the band’s EP “Ниточки карми” (“Threads of Karma”), released in March 2025. Andros has served in the Armed Forces of Ukraine since February 24, 2022, continuing the project’s output alongside his military service. AndrosLand’s new video, “Душа Лісу” (“The Soul of the Forest”), premieres August 8 and will accompany a track destined for the band’s upcoming album, “Hope.”

items.body: Josh da Costa has released the music video for “Shireen,” the final advance track from his solo debut album, “New Wave Graveyard”, out July 24 via Stones Throw. The video, directed by Ambar Navarro, draws on 80s horror movies. Da Costa describes “Shireen” as telling two stories at once: “the feeling of relief after almost breaking up with someone and deciding to stay together – and also sex crazed zombies having an orgy in hell.” For the video, he devised a concept inspired by “bizarre music and sleazy sexy glammy druggy outsiders,” casting the title character Shireen as an alluring woman awaiting her date – and prey. Director Ambar Navarro said the character “targets victims who have powers/talents she absorbs,” adding that many of her references came from B-movie horror films such as “Creepshow.” “New Wave Graveyard” runs 11 tracks: “Skygirl,” “Proving Me Right,” “Cordelia,” “Shireen,” “Tissues,” “Hospital Clown,” “After Your Heart,” “Slip By,” “Sleepy Babe,” “96 Year Old Girl” and “Beach In The Rain.” The album cover art is by Robert Beatty. New Wave Graveyard by Josh da Costa Da Costa said “New Wave Graveyard” follows a period of “getting close to people and getting torn between the types of pleasure and discomfort all of that brings. Breaking people’s hearts but mostly your own. And remaining excited about not just falling in love but staying in love.” Da Costa will perform at the Stones Throw 30th anniversary show on October 16 at the Lodge Room in Los Angeles. About Josh da Costa Josh da Costa is a musician and DJ who hosts the Confusing Mix show on NTS Radio, where he draws on records from Brussels micro-labels, Flying Nun Records favorites and leftfield post-punk. On “Shireen,” he mixes power pop, My Bloody Valentine and Shoes influences. “New Wave Graveyard,” his solo debut album, is released July 24, 2026 via Stones Throw.

items.body: AMP Industrial Festival is coming back to Montreal for a second edition, running October 9 to 11, 2026 at Foufounes Electriques, according to festival listings and the event’s organizers, AMP Industrial Events. The dates are confirmed through the festival’s Bandsintown listing, which places the 2026 run at Foufounes Electriques in Montreal from October 9 through 11. The festival’s own website, amp-festival.com, is currently offline for maintenance. Pat, who handles outreach for AMP Industrial Events, told Side-Line the festival drew a strong contingent of European attendees last year and that the organizers are open to doing interviews ahead of the 2026 edition. 2026 lineup by day Friday, October 9: Echoberyl, Denuit, Mercy Girl, Laura Krieg, Automelodi, The City Gates Saturday, October 10: Chrom, ESA, Ivardensphere, Frontal Boundary, The Marquis Is Dead, Digital Poodle, Creature Sunday, October 11: Statiqbloom, Synapscape, Darkrad, Anarchotech, Some Became Hollow Tubes, S:CAGE, Grief Debt, Property Violator The bill also includes DJ sets from Désordres Sonores, Fleshbot, LCEDP, Anatema, Kasey Riot, Razorgrrl, Mickey Dagger, Davidé, Draris, Neo Edo, Gengis Dhan, LVX x Pat Ze Blue, Melody x Insomniac, Jhnnai and Uriel, with visuals from VJs Tind, Melesul3, Création Ex Nihilo and Bjenski. The 2026 edition is sponsored by L’Au-Delà Diabolik and Berlin. What the first edition looked like AMP Industrial Festival’s debut ran October 10 to 12, 2025, also at Foufounes Electriques, and expanded to 21 live performances across two rooms over three nights, spanning EBM, post-punk, coldwave, IDM, experimental and techno. Headliners included Kontravoid, Encephalon and Ayria, with other confirmed acts including Suicide Commando, Orphx, Ancient Methods, Iszoloscope, NNHMN, Vromb and Thisquietarmy, alongside a DJ program that ran deep into the early hours. About AMP Industrial Events AMP Industrial Events is a Montreal-based organization built around industrial, industrial techno, doomcore, rhythmic noise, IDM and ambient programming, and AMP Fest has functioned as its flagship gathering since the first edition in October 2025. That debut ran across two rooms at Foufounes Electriques, a multi-level venue that opened in 1983 and is regarded as Montreal’s oldest alternative music venue, hosting rock, metal, punk and electronic shows for more than four decades. Foufounes Electriques’ layout, with a main floor and separate concert rooms, has made it a fit for multi-stage events such as AMP Fest, and the venue returns to host the festival’s second edition this October. Ticket details for the October dates have not been announced yet. Side-Line will follow up as AMP Industrial Events confirms ticketing for the 2026 edition.
